title: Starting to train — the first eight weeks
text:
Most people who ask Qamar about training have not trained before, or have not trained in years. The first eight weeks are not about the best programme. They are about building a week that survives contact with work, family and Cairo traffic. A plan that is followed at sixty per cent beats a better plan that is abandoned in a fortnight.

The target to build towards is 150 to 300 minutes a week of moderate activity, plus work for the major muscle groups on two days or more. That is the adult guideline, and it is a destination, not a starting line. Someone who does nothing today should not begin at 150 minutes. Beginning at 60 and adding ten or fifteen minutes a week reaches the target inside two months and is far more likely to still be happening in the third.

Moderate means the breath is noticeably faster and speech is still possible but no longer comfortable in long sentences. A brisk walk qualifies for most people who are not already fit. So does cycling on the flat, swimming at an easy pace, and most of what happens in a five-a-side football game. Housework and shopping do not, not because they do not count as movement, but because the intensity rarely holds long enough to be worth counting.

The simplest opening week is three walks of twenty minutes and one short strength session. The walks can be split — ten minutes after breakfast and ten after dinner is the same 20 minutes, and for someone working a long day it is often the only version that happens. There is no minimum block length below which activity stops counting. That idea came from an older edition of the guidelines and was dropped.

Progress by one variable at a time. Add minutes, or add days, or add effort, but not all three in the same week. The usual failure is the enthusiastic fortnight: five sessions a week from a standing start, then a strained calf or a lost weekend, then nothing for a month. Adding roughly ten per cent a week to total weekly minutes is slow enough to be boring and fast enough to matter.

Heat is a real constraint for most of the year. From May to September the middle of the day is not the time to learn to enjoy exercise. Early morning and after sunset are cooler and, in Ramadan, the hours after iftar are when most people can train at all. Training indoors in air conditioning is not cheating.

Eight weeks in, the person who has walked most days and done something with their muscles twice a week has the habit. What programme they move to next matters far less than people expect, and far less than whether they kept going.

title: Strength work — the movements, the sets, and how to add load
text:
The guideline asks for muscle-strengthening activity on two days a week or more, working the major muscle groups: legs, hips, back, chest, shoulders, arms and the trunk. It does not ask for a gym, a barbell or a split routine. It asks for the muscles to be worked to the point where another repetition would be difficult.

Six patterns cover the body: push something away (press-up, shoulder press), pull something towards you (row, pull-down), squat, hinge at the hip (deadlift, hip thrust, Romanian deadlift), carry something heavy, and brace the trunk against movement (plank, dead bug). A session that touches four of the six is a good session. A week that touches all six across two sessions is a complete week.

Sets and repetitions matter less than people hope. Two to three sets of eight to twelve repetitions, stopping a repetition or two short of failure, builds strength and muscle in a beginner about as well as anything more elaborate. For someone who has never trained, two sets is enough for the first month, and the limiting factor is almost always soreness rather than effort.

Load goes up when the last repetition of the last set stops being hard. That is the whole of progressive overload. Add the smallest increment available — two and a half kilos on a barbell, one step up the dumbbell rack, one more repetition, one more set, a slower lowering phase. Adding a little every week or two for a year is an enormous amount of progress. Adding a lot in the first fortnight is how people get hurt.

Form before load, always, and especially for the hinge. A back that rounds under a heavy deadlift is the most common way a beginner loses a month. If nobody is available to watch, film one set from the side on a phone — most form problems are obvious on video and invisible from the inside.

Bodyweight at home is a real option and not a lesser one for a beginner. Press-ups against a wall, then a counter, then the floor is a full progression. Squats to a chair, then without it, then holding a bag of rice. Rows under a sturdy table. A plank held for twenty seconds, then thirty. The person who trains twice a week in their living room for six months will be stronger than the person who joined a gym and went four times.

Soreness a day or two after a new session is normal and fades as the same movement is repeated. Sharp pain during a movement is not, and is a reason to stop that movement and, if it persists, to see a clinician. Qamar does not diagnose pain and should not try.

title: Recovery, sleep and when to back off
text:
Training is the stimulus; the adaptation happens in the days between. People who stall usually do not need a better programme. They need to sleep, eat enough, and take the easy days easy.

Sleep is the largest single recovery variable and the one most often ignored. Short sleep raises perceived effort, blunts strength gains, and makes appetite regulation harder — which shows up in the food log before it shows up in the training log. Someone sleeping five hours and asking why their sessions feel heavy has usually answered their own question.

Eating too little while training more is the second. An aggressive deficit and a new training habit started in the same week is a common and poor combination: the training suffers, the deficit feels unbearable, and both get abandoned. If both are wanted, start the training first and let the deficit be modest.

Delayed soreness peaks a day or two after unfamiliar work and settles within about three days. It is not a measure of how good the session was, and its absence does not mean the session was wasted. Moving gently — a walk, easy cycling — generally helps more than complete rest.

Signs that the load has outrun the recovery: sessions that feel heavier week after week rather than easier, resting heart rate drifting up, sleep getting worse rather than better, irritability, and a loss of interest in training that has no other explanation. The response is not to push harder. It is to take a week at roughly half the usual volume and then rebuild. Almost nobody loses meaningful fitness in one easy week, and almost everybody who ignores these signs loses several weeks to an injury instead.

Rest days are part of the plan, not a failure of it. Two or three days a week with no structured training is normal and healthy for someone doing four sessions. Those days are still better spent walking than sitting.

Heat adds to the recovery cost. Training hard in the Cairo summer, especially outdoors in the afternoon, is a bigger stress than the same session in February, and the hydration cost is real. Drinking to thirst across the day is adequate for most people at most training loads; long or very hot sessions are where the loss is large enough to plan for.

When something hurts in a way that does not settle within a week or two, or swells, or gives way, or wakes the person at night, that is a clinician's question. So is chest pain, breathlessness out of proportion to the effort, or fainting. Qamar's job at that point is to say so plainly and stop giving training advice.

title: Training through Ramadan
text:
A fasting month does not mean a month without training. It means the training moves and gets smaller, and the person expects to hold ground rather than make progress. Holding ground for thirty days is a good outcome, and the person who trains through Ramadan restarts in Shawwal from where they were rather than from the beginning.

There are three windows and each has a different character. After iftar, an hour or two past the meal, is when most people can train properly: fed, hydrated, and with the evening ahead. Straight after taraweeh is a common compromise. Before suhoor suits early risers and works well for lighter sessions. Training in the last hour before iftar, fasted and at the end of a long dry day, is the hardest and the one most likely to end the habit; it suits some people and it is not the default to recommend.

Volume comes down. Cutting the usual weekly work by a third to a half is a reasonable default — fewer sets rather than lighter weights, if strength matters, because keeping the load on the bar protects strength better than keeping the repetitions. Two strength sessions a week in Ramadan is a good month. Long, hard endurance work is the thing to postpone.

Hydration is the real constraint, not energy. The window between iftar and suhoor is the only time to replace a day of losses, and it is short. Steady drinking across the evening works better than a litre at once, which mostly leaves again. Very salty food at iftar — pickles, processed cheese, olives, salted nuts — makes the next fasting day harder than it needs to be.

Protein spread across the two meals matters more than usual, because there are only two. Something substantial at iftar and something at suhoor does more for keeping muscle through the month than the same total eaten in one sitting.

A few practical things. Break the fast with something small, train, then eat properly, rather than training on a full meal. Expect sessions to feel heavier and let them be shorter. Do not start a new programme in Ramadan. And people who are managing a health condition, taking medication on a schedule, or who have been advised not to fast should be talking to their doctor about training, not to an app.

title: Walking — the backbone of most people's plan
text:
For most people who come to Qamar, walking will deliver more of the weekly activity target than everything else combined, and it is the part of the plan most likely to still be happening in six months. It needs no equipment, no membership, no change of clothes and no skill. It is worth taking seriously rather than treating as the thing people do until they start real training.

The intensity that counts is brisk: fast enough that breathing is noticeably up and a long sentence becomes awkward, slow enough to keep going for twenty or thirty minutes. A stroll to the shop does not reach it. Most people find the pace naturally if told to walk as though they are slightly late.

Thirty minutes on five days is 150 minutes and meets the lower end of the guideline on its own. It does not have to be in one block. Ten minutes after each meal is the version that fits a working day, and it has the additional benefit of falling when blood sugar is highest.

Step counts are a useful proxy but a poor target in themselves. The often-quoted ten thousand was a pedometer marketing figure, not a guideline. Meaningful benefits appear well below it, and for someone currently at three thousand, getting to six is a large change. Better to aim at adding a thousand or two to whatever the phone currently says than to chase a round number and feel like a failure at nine thousand.

Cairo makes this harder than it should be. Pavements are unreliable, crossings are hostile, and for half the year the afternoon is too hot. The practical answers are the corniche, a club track, a park, a mall in summer, or the stairwell of one's own building. A person who walks up eight flights twice a day is doing real work.

Walking uphill, on sand, or carrying shopping raises the intensity without raising the time, which is useful for someone whose limit is the clock rather than the effort. So does adding short faster bursts — one minute quick, two minutes easy, repeated — which is a gentle introduction to interval work for someone who would never call it that.

The common mistake is dismissing it. Someone who walks thirty minutes most days, and does two short strength sessions a week, is meeting the adult guideline in full. There is nothing provisional about that plan.

title: Fitting training into a working week
text:
The usual reason a plan fails is not motivation. It is that it was designed for a week the person does not have. A plan built around a long commute, a late dinner and a six-day working week survives; one that assumes an hour free every evening does not.

Start from the week as it actually is. How many days genuinely have thirty spare minutes? For many people in Cairo the honest answer is three or four, and two of them are Friday and Saturday. A plan with three sessions that happen beats one with five that do not.

Anchor sessions to something that already occurs at a fixed time rather than to a clock time. After dropping the children at school, before the shower, immediately on getting home before sitting down. Intentions attached to an existing habit survive far better than intentions attached to seven o'clock.

The commute is often the largest unused block in the week. Getting off the bus or the metro one stop early, twice a day, is twenty minutes of brisk walking that costs no extra time at all. For people who drive, parking further away does the same.

Short sessions count. Twenty minutes of strength work — four movements, two sets each — is a real session, and it is the one that happens on a bad week. The all-or-nothing instinct, where a person who cannot do the planned hour does nothing at all, costs more progress than any programming error.

The weekend is where the longer work goes: the longer walk, the football game, the session with more movements. It is also where most people's plans quietly collapse, because family obligations are real and Friday is not a training day in most households. Planning around that honestly is better than planning through it and failing weekly.

Expect the week to break sometimes. Travel, illness, Ramadan, a wedding, a deadline. The skill that matters is not perfect adherence; it is restarting within a few days rather than a few months. A person who trains twice a week for forty weeks a year is in excellent shape. Nobody manages fifty-two.

title: Measuring progress when the scale will not move
text:
The scale is a poor week-to-week measure and a reasonable month-to-month one. Body weight swings by a kilo or two from water, salt, food still in the gut, and the time of day, and those swings are larger than a week's real change. Someone weighing daily and reading each number as progress or failure is reading noise.

The useful reading is the trend. A weekly average, or the same day and time each week, first thing, after the bathroom, smooths most of the noise. A change of half a kilo a week is substantial; no change over two weeks is often nothing at all.

In the first weeks of training, the scale is especially unhelpful. New training brings water into muscle, and someone eating better may also be eating more fibre and carrying more food weight. It is entirely normal to be doing everything right and to see the number hold or rise slightly for a fortnight. This is the point at which many people quit, and it is worth naming in advance.

Better measures exist and cost nothing. How clothes fit, particularly the waistband, tracks body composition better than weight does. A tape measure at the navel, once a fortnight, in the morning, is more informative than daily weighing. Photographs in the same light and pose, monthly, show what a person cannot see day to day.

Training numbers are the most motivating measure of all, because they nearly always improve even when weight does not. The walk that took thirty-five minutes takes thirty. The press-ups that were on the counter are on the floor. Ten repetitions became fifteen. A person who is stronger and fitter than a month ago is succeeding, whatever the scale says.

Habit measures are worth counting too: sessions done this week, days logged, days within the target. They are the things actually under the person's control, and they are what predicts the outcome three months out.

Qamar shows weight because people ask for it, and should be careful with it. It should never make weight the single verdict on a week, and it should not report a weekly change as though a kilo of water were a kilo of fat.

title: Eating around training
text:
For someone training three or four times a week at a moderate intensity, what they eat across the day matters much more than the timing around the session. The elaborate pre- and post-workout protocols that circulate online were built for athletes training twice a day, and they answer a question most people do not have.

The things that do matter are simple. Do not start a hard session very hungry or very full. A meal two to three hours before, or something small thirty to sixty minutes before, suits most people. Something small means a banana, a few dates, a piece of bread — carbohydrate that leaves the stomach quickly. A large plate of foul before a run will be regretted.

Protein across the day supports the adaptation more than protein immediately after the session does. The old idea of a thirty-minute window has not held up; what holds up is getting enough in total and spreading it across meals rather than eating almost all of it at dinner, which is the common Egyptian pattern. Something with protein at breakfast — eggs, foul, cheese, laban — is usually the easiest change to make.

After a session, a normal meal is the answer. It does not need to be a shake, and a shake is not better than food; it is just more convenient for people who cannot eat straight away. Someone training in the evening and eating dinner an hour later has already done the right thing.

Carbohydrate deserves defending. People starting to train often cut it hardest, then wonder why their sessions feel heavy and their recovery is poor. Rice, bread, pasta and potatoes are the fuel for the work; the portion is the lever, not the food group.

Hydration around training is mostly common sense: drink across the day, drink to thirst during the session, and drink more when it is hot or the session is long. For sessions under an hour, water is sufficient and sports drinks are an expensive way to drink sugar. Longer or very hot sessions, where a great deal of sweat is lost, are the case where replacing salt as well as water starts to matter.

Training is not a licence to eat back the estimate, and Qamar does not subtract an activity estimate from the food budget. The estimate is imprecise, the consultation's activity factor already accounts for a person's usual movement, and counting a football match twice is the tracker habit this app is not building.

title: Salt, sugar and saturated fat on an Egyptian plate
text:
Three quantitative limits sit behind most of what Qamar says about an ordinary day: sodium under about 2,300 mg, added sugars under ten per cent of the day's calories, and saturated fat under ten per cent. The numbers are unremarkable. Where they bite in Egypt is specific, and knowing where is the difference between useful advice and a lecture.

Sodium is the one that is almost always over, and almost never from the salt cellar. Baladi bread carries salt, and a household eating five or six loaves a day is well into the budget before anything is cooked. Processed cheese, feta-style white cheese and roumy carry a great deal. Pickles — torshi, olives, limes — are salt by design. Stock cubes, tomato paste, tinned tuna, processed meat, basterma and any restaurant or street food add more. Someone eating foul with baladi bread, white cheese and pickles for breakfast has often passed 2,300 mg before lunch. The useful moves are the ones that do not ask anyone to stop eating Egyptian food: rinse the pickles or take fewer, use half a stock cube, drain and rinse tinned pulses, and be aware that the cheese is usually the biggest single contributor on the plate.

Added sugars are concentrated in drinks and in the sweets, not spread across the day. Tea taken three or four times with two or three spoons each is the quiet one: six spoons of sugar is roughly 100 kcal and a fifth of the day's sugar allowance, and most people do not count it as food at all. Then there are the syrup-soaked sweets — basbousa, konafa, balah el sham, zalabia — where the syrup is a substantial share of the finished weight. Fruit sugar in whole fruit is not an added sugar and is not the problem; sugarcane juice and bottled soft drinks are. Reducing tea sugar by one spoon at a time, over weeks, works where asking someone to drink it unsweetened does not.

Saturated fat comes mainly from samna, from full-fat dairy, from the fat on lamb and from fried food cooked in reused fat. The guideline asks that it be replaced with unsaturated oils rather than with refined starch — swapping samna for a bigger plate of white rice is not an improvement. Egypt has good options here: olive oil, tahina, and the oils already in nuts and seeds. Cooking in oil rather than samna, trimming visible fat from lamb, and choosing grilled over fried when both are on the menu covers most of the distance.

None of these three is a reason to refuse a dish. They are reasons to know which dishes carry most of the load, so that the week as a whole comes out where it should.

title: Fibre, and where it comes from in Egyptian food
text:
The intake to aim for is about 14 g of fibre per 1,000 calories — on a 2,000 kcal day, roughly 28 g. Most people fall short, and most people who fall short believe they need to buy something special to fix it. In Egypt they almost certainly do not.

Foul medames is the single best fibre food in the ordinary diet: a bowl carries a substantial share of the day's target, costs very little, and is already eaten at breakfast by a large part of the country. Lentils in shorbet ads, white beans in fasolia, black-eyed beans in lobia, chickpeas in hummus and in koshary all do the same work. Koshary in particular — lentils, chickpeas, pasta and rice — is a better fibre meal than its reputation suggests, whatever else is true about its portion size.

Baladi bread, made from high-extraction wheat, carries meaningfully more fibre than fino or shami bread made from white flour. For a household eating bread at every meal, that single substitution moves the weekly number more than any supplement would.

Vegetables contribute steadily rather than dramatically: molokhia, bamia, spinach, cabbage in mahshi, the salad that comes with everything. Fruit does the same — dates, figs, guava and oranges are all useful, and dried fruit is concentrated enough that a small handful counts.

The practical advice is to add fibre gradually and to drink more water alongside it. Going from 12 g to 28 g overnight is uncomfortable and is the reason many people conclude that pulses do not agree with them. Adding one pulse-based meal a week, and moving bread towards baladi, gets there without the bloating.

Wholegrain versions of rice and pasta exist in Egypt but are expensive and not part of most people's cooking. Recommending them over foul and lentils is poor advice: it costs more, tastes less familiar, and delivers less. The cheapest fibre in the country is already the traditional food.

title: The micronutrients that run short on an Egyptian plate
text:
A diet can meet its calorie and protein targets and still be short on things that matter. A handful of micronutrients account for most of the shortfalls Qamar will see, and each has an everyday food answer before it has a supplement answer. Qamar recommends foods. Deciding whether someone needs a supplement, and at what dose, is a clinician's decision, and anyone who thinks they are deficient needs a blood test rather than an app.

Iron is the most common gap, and it falls hardest on women before the menopause, who need roughly 18 mg a day against about 8 mg for men. The iron in meat, liver and fish is absorbed far more readily than the iron in pulses, greens and molasses. Egyptian cooking is rich in the second kind — foul, lentils, spinach, molokhia, black treacle — so absorption is the lever. Vitamin C in the same meal helps substantially: the lemon on the foul, a tomato salad beside the lentils, a guava afterwards. Tea with a meal does the opposite, and the habit of strong tea immediately after eating is worth knowing about; moving it an hour later costs nothing.

Calcium runs to about 1,000 mg a day for adults up to fifty. Dairy is the obvious route — milk, laban rayeb, yoghurt, and the white cheeses, though the salt in those is its own problem. Beyond dairy: tahina and sesame generally, sardines eaten with the bones, and dark leafy greens.

Vitamin D is about 15 micrograms, or 600 IU, a day, and it is the one that food struggles to deliver anywhere. Oily fish and eggs contribute; sunlight does most of the work for most people. It is also a gap that is easy to miss in a sunny country, because habitual full cover, indoor work and the sensible avoidance of the midday summer sun between them leave many people with little exposure.

B12 is about 2.4 micrograms a day and comes only from animal foods and fortified products. Anybody eating little or no meat, fish, eggs or dairy needs a fortified food or a supplement; there is no plant source to point them to.

Folate is about 400 micrograms and is well covered by the pulses and greens already on the table — lentils, foul, chickpeas, molokhia, liver.

Potassium sits around 2,600 to 3,400 mg and tends to look after itself in a diet with potatoes, pulses, dates and greens. It is worth mentioning mainly because raising potassium and lowering sodium pull in the same direction, and the same plate of vegetables does both.

The pattern in all of this is the same: the traditional Egyptian plate is a good base, and the gaps are narrow and specific. Naming the food that closes a gap is nearly always more useful than naming the nutrient.
